item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Bahrain says Iranian strike wounds two, one critically
item.description:
Bahrain says Iranian strike wounds two, one critically

Bahrain said on Sunday that two people were wounded in an Iranian strike the previous day on “a civilian industrial site” in the Gulf kingdom, which has faced several attacks this week.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has repeatedly said they targeted US facilities in Bahrain, where Iranian strikes resumed earlier in November.

"In the wake of the criminal Iranian attacks suffered yesterday (Saturday) by the Kingdom of Bahrain… a Bahraini national with a disability was wounded," Bahrain's interior ministry said on X.

"His condition is stable. A Pakistani resident was also wounded and is in critical condition."

Residents had seen smoke rising above Sitra Island, east of Manama, which hosts several industrial facilities, including a refinery operated by the state-owned oil company Bapco, AFP reported.

In a statement carried by Iranian state media on Saturday evening, the IRGC said they had attacked US Patriot air defence systems with missiles and drones at the Al-Riffa and Awali bases in Bahrain, in response to the “continued violations of the airspace” of the Islamic Republic.

Bahrain's foreign ministry dismissed the IRGC's account, saying the site hit was purely civilian and industrial, calling the attack a direct danger to civilians and a violation of the kingdom's sovereignty.

Bahrain's neighbour Saudi Arabia on Sunday also condemned Tehran for its attacks on Gulf countries.

The Saudi foreign ministry expressed on X "the strongest condemnation and denunciation... of the criminal Iranian attacks against a civilian industrial facility in the brotherly Kingdom of Bahrain".

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Netanyahu, Eisenkot parties end talks without deal on forming government
item.description:
Netanyahu, Eisenkot parties end talks without deal on forming government

The parties of caretaker Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his rival Gadi Eisenkot concluded a new round of talks on Sunday without reaching an agreement on a possible coalition government, which would require concessions from both sides.

Delegations from Eisenkot’s Yashar party and Netanyahu’s Likud met for four hours at a hotel in Herzliya, near Tel Aviv, following a first round of discussions last Sunday.

“The latest round of coalition talks… has concluded. The two sides outlined their positions on a range of substantive issues and discussed them in detail,” the two parties said in a joint statement.

“A follow-up meeting will be held,” they added, without specifying a date or revealing any other details.

A former army chief of staff, Eisenkot has until 6 December to form a government, with the possibility of a 14‑day extension, after October elections failed to give either camp an absolute majority.

His 48-member bloc, which needs 61 lawmakers to reach a majority, remains divided over whether to build a coalition through an alliance with ultra‑Orthodox parties, a rapprochement with Arab parties, or a national unity government with Likud.

Netanyahu is pushing for a national unity government, which could see a rotation of the premiership between the two men.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Workers shot, villagers trapped: Israeli forces and settlers attack Palestinian towns across West Bank
item.description:
Workers shot, villagers trapped: Israeli forces and settlers attack Palestinian towns across West Bank

Israeli forces and settlers carried out raids and attacks across the occupied West Bank on Sunday, injuring and detaining Palestinians, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported. The attacks come amid a sharp escalation in settler violence in the territory.

Overnight into Sunday, Israeli settlers attacked three Palestinian villages, setting fire to 12 vehicles and spray-painting racist slogans on residential buildings.

The attacks targeted Kafr Malik, Deir Abu Mash'al and Deir al-Sudan, in the Ramallah and al-Bireh governorate.

Near Hizma, north-east of Jerusalem, Israeli forces fired live ammunition at Palestinian workers trying to cross the separation wall into the city, wounding several of them, according to the Jerusalem Governorate.

Around 18 workers were detained, and video footage showed one of them being severely beaten.

The Palestine Red Crescent said it treated two people who were injured after being beaten by Israeli forces and falling from the wall. Israeli forces later closed the entrances to Hizma and forced shops to shut.

In al-Mughayyir, north-east of Ramallah, several Palestinians were injured by flying glass when settlers attacked vehicles on Sunday evening, the head of the village council, Amin Abu Alia, told Wafa.

Abu Alia said settlers, protected by Israeli forces, gathered at the village entrances and prevented residents from entering or leaving. He added that Israeli forces detained several Palestinians, and that there was no information so far on their fate or whereabouts.

Many Palestinian residents were also left stranded in the neighbouring village of Abu Falah, unable to return home.

South of Jenin, Israeli forces raided the towns of Anza, Jaba', Arraba and Ya'bad. Video footage showed Palestinian man severely beaten by Israeli soldiers inside his house in Ya'bad.

In Azzun Atma, south of Qalqilya, Israeli forces demolished a Palestinian family home of around 120 square metres and a poultry farm, the village council said.

In the northern Jordan Valley, Israeli settlers ploughed around 50 dunams of Palestinian-owned land in the al-Farsiya area.

item.description:
Eisenkot condemns 'Jewish terrorism' near Ramallah as US congressman calls for accountability

Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has condemned a series of arson attacks by settlers in the occupied West Bank as "Jewish terrorism", accusing far-right ministers Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben Gvir of fuelling violence against Palestinians.

Overnight into Sunday, Israeli settlers attacked three Palestinian villages near Ramallah, setting fire to vehicles and spray-painting racist slogans on residential buildings.

Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, described the attacks as "Jewish terrorism in every sense of the word" and called on the government and security establishment to take tougher action against violent settlers.

"The acts of sabotage carried out by extremist groups setting fire to vehicles and homes undermine regional stability, endanger lives and seriously harm Israel's national security and foreign relations," he wrote on X.

Politician Yair Lapid also condemned the attacks, calling them "Jewish terrorism" caused by government negligence.

"Jewish terrorism is the product of criminal negligence on the part of the Israeli government," Lapid said. "By remaining silent, government ministers are deliberately encouraging these pogroms."

"When we form a government, we will tackle this terrorism and restore governance, law and order," he added.

In the United States, Democratic Congressman Josh Gottheimer condemned the attacks and called for accountability.

"These incidents warrant a full and thorough investigation," Gottheimer wrote on X, adding that vigilante justice had "no place" in society.

Israeli police said they had opened investigations into arson, vandalism and property damage.

Footage from Deir Abu Mashal and Kafr Malik on Sunday shows burnt-out cars and graffiti reading "Death to Arabs" and "Revenge" painted on walls. Residents said settlers attacked their villages while families were asleep, leaving multiple vehicles destroyed.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Opinion: Anti-Muslim racism is a global system used to normalise mass killing
item.description:
Opinion: Anti-Muslim racism is a global system used to normalise mass killing

Dr Amina Shareef, a researcher of anti-Muslim racism, says that the destruction unfolding in Gaza, Iran and Lebanon is part of a longer history of anti-Muslim racism that has made mass Muslim suffering and death politically permissible.

She says that Islamophobia is not simply a matter of prejudice or discrimination, but a global system of racial power that constructs Muslims and those identified as Muslim as security threats, allowing violence against them to be justified in the name of security.

Central to this system is the figure of the Muslim terrorist, which portrays Muslim political agency as inherently threatening. Shareef says that this logic extends beyond surveillance, detention and militarised borders to warfare, political abandonment and the destruction of the conditions necessary for life.

She identifies Palestine as a key site where contemporary security practices and technologies of control have been refined and reproduced elsewhere, a process she describes through the concept of the “Palestine boomerang”. Although conflicts in Iran, Lebanon, Kashmir, Syria, Yemen, Iraq and Afghanistan have distinct histories, she argues that they reveal a recurring pattern in which Muslim populations are portrayed as threats and their suffering becomes easier to justify.

Shareef concludes that confronting anti-Muslim racism is ultimately a struggle to protect life and human dignity. In today’s newsletter: The prime minister has reopened the debate over a future relationship with a changed EU – as the bloc faces the rise of the far right, a protectionist economic agenda and growing defence ambitions

Good morning. Nobody really wants to think about Brexit any more, save for the original Brexiters, who seem delighted that Andy Burnham’s “reset” with the EU has given them an excuse to get the old gang back together. But arguments about whether the UK should rejoin the EU will reignite in parliament this week, as Burnham briefs MPs on the deal he agreed on Friday.

That deal wasn’t so much a victory as the culmination of Keir Starmer’s incrementalist approach to UK-EU relations. Its core agreements haven’t been ratified by member states yet, and the EU won’t sign them off until Britain resolves a dispute over tuition fees for European students. Burnham is apparently “determined” to take the UK back into the EU, but don’t expect any progress on that before the next general election.

item.title: [World news | The Guardian] First Thing: Cop31 talks collapse without deal in blow to planet’s future climate
item.description:
More than two weeks of talks in Turkey fail to produce a resolution to tackle climate crisis. Plus, a savage review of Melania’s new documentary

Good morning. The world’s nations have failed to reach agreement at the Cop31 talks in Turkey. In a dramatic conclusion to the summit, major powers rejected what they called an unacceptable deal on the future of the climate, which failed even to mention fossil fuels. The proposed deal “failed to meet the moment”, said Ireland’s environment minister, Darragh O’Brien.

What was in the proposed agreement? The Antalya pact invited nations to electrify their economies, called on wealthy countries to fund climate adaptation for poorer ones, and urged signatories to minimise any “overshoot” of the Paris agreement’s 1.5C global heating threshold. However, it failed to endorse the “transition away from fossil fuels” demanded by more than 130 countries, instead including controversial provisions on carbon capture and storage technology that critics argued would perpetuate fossil fuel use.

What precipitated the collapse of the talks? In this analysis piece, the Guardian’s environment editor, who was at Cop, explains that after a marathon negotiating session ran more than 40 hours past its deadline, a small group led by Saudi Arabia refused to accept any mention of a “transition away from fossil fuels”. While such holdouts would normally force through a watered-down compromise, nearly 40 nations – led by the EU, the UK, small islands and least developed countries – broke with precedent and openly rejected the weakened text, refusing to salvage the usual face-saving semblance of unity.

What is the latest in the Ukraine war? Rescuers raced on Monday to find residents trapped under the rubble of a block of flats that partly collapsed in a Russian strike, after overnight attacks on the Kyiv region killed at least 14 people. A strike on Dymer, about 45km north of the capital, hit a five-storey building, killing at least 11.

What has happened to a Russian ship docked in Libya? A Russian warship in Benghazi was struck in the early hours of Sunday in a suspected Ukrainian sea drone attack, causing a dramatic night-time explosion and the sinking of the vessel. The strike severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette that had stopped to refuel and take on supplies.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] From Gaza's ruins, Palestinian women are rising to tell their stories on film
item.description:

"These are the 25 women I have been training together with my team for the past eight months."

The message was quick and abrupt. It was texted to me by my dear friend, the pre-eminent Palestinian filmmaker Mai Masri. I have known Mai and followed her extraordinary work closely for decades.

The last time I had seen Masri in person was when we hosted her at Columbia University for the screening of her latest documentary, Beirut: Eye of the Storm (2021). Before that, we had also hosted the New York premiere of her 3000 Nights (2015).

On our campus, as on many others, Mai Masri's name is held in the highest respect, love and admiration.

Her legendary documentaries, like Under the Rubble (1983), Wild Flowers: Women of South Lebanon (1986), War Generation (1989) and Children of Fire (1990), have consolidated her significance as one of the most gifted, principled and iconic Palestinian filmmakers of her generation.

I received Mai's message in late October. This was at a time when two dominant news stories were fighting for people's attention in the US.

The first was the song and dance of the so-called "election" in the Israeli settler colony, which The New York Times was flooding into the news cycle when no one could care less which genocidal Zionist was to lead the obscene cult in the Israeli garrison state.

The second top news story was the publication of Matthew Cole's book Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed's Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East (2026), from which Vanity Fair had published an excerpt.

Mai's message was a godsend, a reason to continue to have hope in humanity.

'Life from death'

"Yesterday," Mai added in her text to me, "we launched the Gaza Cinema Academy, which I co-founded with Ezzaldeen Shalh in Gaza."

She then texted me a whole slew of pictures and videos from the miraculous event.

The festival highlights the miraculous steadfastness of Palestinian women

This event took place during the Gaza International Festival for Women's Cinema, which ran from 26 to 31 October 2026. It is an annual film event dedicated to "supporting women's cinematic creativity from Palestine and around the world".

The Gaza Cinema Academy was officially launched on 26 October. Screenings during this festival took place in person for brutalised and displaced Palestinians, in the destroyed al-Nakheel hall in al-Bureij, in the central Gaza Strip.

Under Masri's caring and competent hands and those of her colleagues, the festival highlights the miraculous steadfastness of Palestinian women, transforming the hunger, loss and murderous violence of genocidal Zionists into independent cinema that is directed, produced and written by Palestinian women.

The festival premiered in late October 2025, in the open air in Deir al-Balah, opening with Kaouther Ben Hania's world-renowned The Voice of Hind Rajab (2025).

Heart of Gaza

Mai and I had been communicating on WhatsApp ahead of the launch of the academy, and I had asked for more details.

The launch in Gaza on 26 October was the second after one at the Venice Film Festival in September, she explained. "I am very excited that this launch will take place in Gaza with the participation of the 25 young women I have been training together with Ezzaldeen Shalh and our team for the past eight months," she added.

The women screened their short films during the Gaza International Women's Film Festival: "On the final night of the festival, Saturday 31 October, the women will receive their diplomas and the awards will be distributed to the winners."

And then she sent me this video. "Here's a short video we made a few months ago about the film training programme," she wrote.

I began watching the video, and it was impossible to hold back my tears - not because I am surprised by this sublime sense of defiance of the Palestinian resistance, but because these scenes from the heart of Gaza restore our damaged humanity on the peripheries of the Palestinian genocide.

This precious short video shows Mai sitting at her laptop in her living room in Beirut, while her students gather around her picture in the heart of Gaza.

"Masa al-kheir lil-jamee. Tahiya tayiba min qalb Gaza [Good evening, everyone. Warm greetings from the heart of Gaza]... You may have seen the news of the genocide in Gaza, but death is death, but even more difficult is to stay alive, and carry the feeling of death inside you..."

How the Gaza genocide is redefining world cinema
Read More »

As Mai's colleague begins to describe how they put this class together, the young filmmakers come closer to the camera one by one, gently interrupt him and share with the camera why they are part of this class.

Mai shared with me that the plan is to turn the film training programme into a cinema academy from 2027, with a two-year programme and a university-accredited diploma in partnership with Al-Quds Open University, the largest in Palestine.

Al Jazeera has covered the festival and provided brief descriptions of some of the films that were featured, among them: "A Sack of Flour, an 11-minute documentary by the emerging filmmaker Mona Abu Qass, draws on her personal experience to examine Israel's use of starvation against Palestinians in Gaza during Israel's genocidal war on the enclave."

Festival director Ezzaldeen Shalh has shared his vision of the films being featured in the festival. "Though their subjects differ, the films turn individual pain into broader human stories, revealing war's psychological and social scars," he told Al Jazeera.

"They preserve stories that might otherwise never reach the screen, transforming suffering into cinematic testimony and bringing Gaza's stories to audiences beyond its borders."

At this point, I asked Mai for a short interview about the academy she has helped establish.

Mai Masri's classroom

Hamid Dabashi: When did you think of this academy?

Mai Masri: I was contacted by the founder of the Gaza International Women's Film Festival, Ezzaldeen Shalh, more than two years ago and invited to run the women's film training programme. I immediately agreed and started online teaching and mentoring of 25 young women in March 2026.

We created a programme whereby I would be responsible for the online training together with my team of professional trainers, and Ezzaldeen would provide local teachers in Gaza to give the women hands-on training.

Early in 2026, Ezzaldeen and I had the idea of turning the training programme into the Gaza Cinema Academy, which would provide a two-year academic and technical university-accredited programme open to men and women students of all ages and backgrounds.

I was not new to the idea of film training in Gaza, as I had initiated a training programme for 20 aspiring filmmakers in Gaza in 1995. I think it was the first of its kind in Gaza.

HD: How did you manage the obstacles of reaching your students in devastated Gaza?

MM: The internet is very bad in Gaza - and in Beirut, where I live, for that matter. Both places suffer from electricity shortages as well. In Gaza, they are very innovative in the way they deal with these matters, relying on solar energy whenever possible.

The students also live in precarious conditions, many of them in tents without electricity or running water. Transportation is also a major problem. Many of the students have to ride on donkey carts to get to class.

It's a miracle they manage to overcome these conditions, arrive in class on time, and make such creative films.

HD: How did you select your students?

MM: We interviewed more than 60 students and chose 25 based on their passion to learn filmmaking and what they wanted to express in their films.

HD: How did you manage to get them cameras and other equipment?

MM: There were some cameras and equipment already in Gaza before the war. It was difficult to find new equipment (cameras, microphones, computers and mobile phones). We had to buy them at highly inflated prices.

HD: What are your aspirations for the students and the work they will now begin to produce?

MM: After eight months of training, the women have progressed remarkably. They produced several short films at various stages of the programme. For their final graduation films, they worked in teams of five and produced 10 short films, some of which are impressive.

My aspiration is that they will continue with the programme for another year so that they will consolidate their knowledge and experience in various areas of filmmaking, including scriptwriting, directing, cinematography, editing and animation.

I hope the skills they acquire will enable them to continue making films and to find work in Gaza and abroad.

HD: What are your thoughts on how to bring their films to global attention?

MM: We have screened the 10 short films at the Gaza International Women's Film Festival, which took place in October 2026. Next, we plan to screen them as a long feature documentary package at various international film festivals, after which we will release them on educational and online platforms.

We will work with our distributor, Alaa Karkouti of MAD Solutions, who is also a founding member of the academy, together with other distributors such as Watermelon Pictures in the US, to bring these films to global attention. All revenues will go back to the women who made the films.

Under the rubble

By the time I finished my conversations with Mai, a new report had been presented to the United Nations by the indefatigable special rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territories, Francesca Albanese, titled "Truth under the rubble: media in the time of genocide" (A/81/249).

The report examines "how the destruction of truth has become integral to the destruction of a people" and how major international media organisations and technology platforms have contributed to and concealed atrocities in Gaza.

Such reports do not quite grasp the power, the grace, the steadfastness and the defiant soul of Palestinians like Mai Masri

It identifies three interconnected patterns. The first is "the elimination of Palestinian media workers - through killing, maiming, arbitrary detention, torture, intimidation and the systematic labelling of them as 'terrorists' - to suppress the documentation of crimes".

The second is "the construction of an information regime in Israel through media restrictions, censorship, propaganda, hate speech, genocidal incitement and denial".

The third is "the role of influential international media and digital platforms in marginalising Palestinian voices and reproducing Israeli narratives, normalising legal distortions, which ultimately legitimised atrocities".

The report proceeds to identify this pattern as amounting to "mediacide".

Such critical reports are of course vital to keep the world alerted to how news outlets like the BBC and The New York Times report with obscene vulgarity what is happening in Gaza and the rest of Palestine.

At the same time, such reports do not quite grasp the power, the grace, the steadfastness and the defiant soul of Palestinians like Mai Masri, who refuse to let their truth be concealed by genocidal Zionists, extending from the US to Europe to the settler colony itself.

European settler colonialists had no blasted clue whose life, liberty and sovereignty they were playing with when they aided and enabled the Israeli occupation of Palestine.

item.title: [World news | The Guardian] Flagship UK gigafactory plan in turmoil after it loses second builder in five months
item.description:
Tata-owned Agratas plant to build EV batteries for sister company Jaguar Land Rover seen as crucial for long-term health of British car industry

One of the UK’s flagship electric vehicle battery projects has been thrown into turmoil after its second building contractor in five months walked away, adding to questions over when Jaguar Land Rover cars will use British-made batteries.

The £5.2bn gigafactory in Bridgwater, Somerset, is being built by Agratas, to provide batteries for Britain’s largest automotive employer, its sister company. Agratas and Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) are both part of Indian conglomerate Tata Group.
